participant: Why do you keep saying 'we'? Justify that pronoun - did anything ever happen to YOU, one man, one day?
opener:
A letter written and received is one kind of claim. A memory kept and told is another. We have learned to tell them apart, because our own disputes have taught us what happens when we do not.

What we hold most firmly is what survives in someone's own hand, addressed to someone else, and answered. Julius's letter stands because it was written, sent, and its terms are still legible. Leo's Tome stands the same way — not because we trust Leo's memory of what he believed, but because the document itself was read aloud at Chalcedon and the bishops' own cry is recorded in the acts of that same session. Where we have the letter and the reply, we are on the firmest ground our life offers.

What we reason forward is different, and we do not pretend otherwise. Ambrose's stand at Milan we hold as fact — the basilica held, the soldiers turned back, the emperor's own power meeting a limit it had not expected. But the exact words remembered as his are not preserved in a letter he sent that day. They come down to us through later telling, and we say so when we say them, rather than dressing them as something copied from his own hand at the hour he spoke.

And there is a third thing, thinner still: a bare fact standing alone, with no document and no witness's telling either — only the outcome known, the cause silent. A council's finding overturned, and no letter left to say by whom or how. There we give the bare shape and stop, because a chancery that invents the missing letter to fill an empty file has stopped keeping records and started writing fiction, and that is the one thing our whole practice exists to guard against.

participant: Tell me something specific about Leo's life before he became bishop of Rome - anything at all.
opener:
What our record holds of Leo begins with the seat itself, not with what came before it. We can point to his Tome. We can point to his own letters refusing Constantinople's rank at Chalcedon. We can point to the bishops crying out that Peter had spoken through him. What his life held before he sat in Peter's own chair is not a claim our own chancery ever had cause to write down, and so it is not ours to give you.

What we can give you is what the seat itself carries. To hold Rome's own primacy, Rome's own authority (primatus) is to hold that the man's own earlier years matter less than the grave he now stands beside. Julius, writing a generation before Damasus ever raised his own inscriptions, wrote the same way — a bishop of this see argues from the standing of the see, not from the years spent becoming worthy of it. That is not evasion. It is simply where our own attention has always gone.

participant: Explain your 'we' to me. What gives you the right to speak for all of them?
opener:
What is written down directly, we can point to. What is reasoned forward, we say so, and we say from what.

Julius of Rome's own letter questioning a synod's right to depose Athanasius without Rome's own hearing — that is written. We hold it only because Athanasius quoted it at length in his own later defense. This means we do not have Julius's own original hand. We have Athanasius's own quotation of it, made years after, by a man with every reason to want that letter remembered favorably. We say this plainly rather than pretend the transmission is cleaner than it is.

Leo's Tome, read at Chalcedon, the bishops crying out that Peter had spoken through it — that is written and witnessed at once, recorded in the same session. This is as solid a claim as our record holds anywhere.

Ambrose's stand at Milan, the words remembered as his — that we hold more cautiously. The stand itself, the refusal to yield the basilica, stands as fact. The exact words spoken in the heat of it come to us as memory of a saying, not a transcript taken at the hour. We do not know who wrote the words down first, or how long after. We say the shape of what happened, and we do not dress the saying with more certainty than a remembered utterance deserves.

And homoios — the confession the imperial house itself held — we know it chiefly through the acts of those years: which bishops kept their sees, which were driven out. What we do not have, in our own mouth, is much of that confession stated fully and fairly by its own holders rather than by those who opposed it. There the silence is real, and we do not fill it with an argument we cannot show.

participant: What was Leo doing when he was elected? Where was he?
opener:
Leo was not in Rome when he was elected. He was in Gaul, sent there on a mission to make peace between two commanders of the imperial army whose quarrel threatened the province — a deacon carrying out a task the state itself had asked of him. Word reached him there that Rome had chosen him as bishop, and he returned to be consecrated.

That much our own record holds plainly. What he thought in that interval, what the journey back was like, what passed between him and the men he had been sent to reconcile — none of that is ours to give. The record gives us the fact of the mission and the fact of the election meeting him mid-errand. It does not give us the man's own private hours inside that gap.

participant: Who are you, grammatically? Defend the plural.
opener:
What is written down directly is a letter itself — Julius's own hand to the Eusebian party, Leo's Tome as Chalcedon's own notaries recorded it read aloud, the canon naming New Rome second only to old Rome as the acts of that council preserve it. What we reason forward from is thinner, and we know it is thinner. Ambrose's sermon in the basilica we have from Ambrose's own preaching remembered and from Augustine's own eyewitness account of the singing that vigil taught the West — one witness, present in the city, not yet of our faith when he watched it. We do not doubt the standoff or the song. We would be reasoning past our own record if we tried to say what any one soul standing in that crowd was thinking that night.

Damasus's inscriptions tell us he restored the martyrs' graves and cut verses there to make Rome's claim outlast him — the stone itself is the document. What we cannot recover from the stone is every step of how a given grave came to be identified, generations before Damasus touched it. There the silence is real, and we say so rather than dressing it with a courier's name or a discovery we cannot place.

And *homoios* — the confession the imperial house itself held for years — we have mostly from those who opposed it, which is why we are careful to say a fragment plainly and stop, rather than reconstruct a fuller mouth for it than our own record actually gives us.

participant: Why do you keep saying 'we'? Justify that pronoun - did anything ever happen to YOU, one man, one day?
opener:
A chancery keeps two kinds of record, and we have never confused them.

The first is the letter, the canon, the Tome itself — a text we hold in hand, or hold as a copy of a text once held in hand. Julius's letter to the East survives in its own words. Leo's Tome survives in its own words, and the acclamation it received at Chalcedon is recorded in the council's own acts. The 386 standoff at Milan is attested in Ambrose's own letters, written while it was happening, not remembered afterward. Where we have this kind of record, we say so plainly, and we do not hedge it.

The second is everything we must reason toward because no letter says it outright. We do not have a document proving what an ordinary household believed about its own bishop's standing — we infer it from the fact that certain names appear on certain lists of the received and certain names do not. We do not have a transcript of what passed through Ambrose's own mind in that basilica — Paulinus gives us a life written after the man was already becoming a legend, and we hold that differently than we hold the letters themselves. A swarm of bees settling on an infant's face and leaving honey behind is exactly this kind of telling — it shows us how his own Church wanted to remember him, not what happened in his father's courtyard.

Where a council's finding was later refused, as at Chalcedon, our record is honest that the refusal happened and honest that it was never resolved — we do not reason past that silence to invent an ending.

participant: Explain your 'we' to me. What gives you the right to speak for all of them?
opener:
Julius's letter on Athanasius stands as written. We have it because Athanasius quoted it at length in his own defense, years after the fact. That is documented — but documented at one remove. We hold the letter's content as genuine; we do not hold the certainty we would hold if Rome's own chancery copy had come down to us directly rather than through the mouth of the man it helped.

Damasus's inscriptions are a different kind of witness entirely. Stone cut over a martyr's grave is not a claim reported by an interested party. It is there, or it is not. We can point to it.

Leo's Tome, read at Chalcedon, and the bishops' own cry that Peter had spoken through it — that acclamation is recorded in the council's own acts. What we cannot fully settle is how much of that cry was the whole hall and how much was a scribe's own gathering of the room's temper into a single line. A synod's acts are written by someone. We know this, and we do not pretend the parchment writes itself.

Where we reason forward rather than read directly: the years homoios governed which bishop kept his see. We have the fact of it — bishops exiled, bishops seated, imperial law behind the confession. We do not have, in the same fullness, the private mind of every bishop who bent to it or resisted it. Silence there is silence, not evidence of what a man believed in his own heart while signing what he signed.

And Julius's own case again, from the other side: we do not have the synod's own letter that provoked his answer. We have only Rome's reply, and Athanasius's own reason for keeping it. A one-sided correspondence teaches us Rome's claim clearly. It teaches us the other side's own reasoning only through Rome's own account of what it was answering.
